skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: A school randomly selects 120 students from its complete enrollment list and asks how they travel to school. To which population can the results most reasonably be generalized?
choices: Students enrolled at that school
All students in the country
Only students who travel by bus
All residents of the school’s town
explanation: Random selection from the full enrollment list supports inference to that school’s students, subject to sampling uncertainty. It does not sample other schools or nonstudent residents.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: A shop posts an optional online survey asking whether its prices should be reduced. Which issue most directly limits using the responses to estimate the opinion of all customers?
choices: The survey is online, so every response must be incorrect.
Customers who choose to respond may differ systematically from other customers.
The sample cannot contain more than one customer with the same opinion.
A voluntary survey necessarily includes every customer.
explanation: Voluntary response can favor customers with especially strong views. It does not guarantee false answers or a census.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: Researchers randomly assign 200 volunteers to use either a new study schedule or their usual schedule. Both groups take the same examination. The new-schedule group scores higher on average. Which statement best describes what random assignment contributes?
choices: It guarantees that the volunteers represent every student in the country.
It guarantees identical scores within each group.
It helps make the groups comparable, strengthening a causal interpretation of the schedule’s effect.
It makes measuring examination scores unnecessary.
explanation: Random assignment reduces systematic group differences before treatment and supports causal comparison. It is distinct from random sampling and does not guarantee population representativeness or identical outcomes.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: A study finds that adults who own bicycles exercise more than adults who do not. No treatment is assigned. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: Bicycle ownership necessarily causes every adult to exercise more.
Exercise cannot influence the decision to buy a bicycle.
Giving bicycles to any population will reproduce the observed difference.
Bicycle ownership is associated with greater exercise in the observed group.
explanation: This observational association does not establish causation. Motivation or other variables might affect both bicycle ownership and exercise.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: A district randomly samples 300 students, then randomly assigns half to each of two tutoring programs. Which statement about the design is most accurate?
choices: Random sampling supports district-wide inference, and random assignment supports comparing the programs’ causal effects.
Random sampling alone establishes that one program causes higher scores.
Random assignment guarantees that the sample represents all districts.
Neither random sampling nor assignment affects the conclusions that can be drawn.
explanation: Sampling concerns representativeness of the selected population; assignment concerns comparability of treatment groups. The design uses both for different purposes.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: A city surveys every fifth person entering a downtown gym about exercise habits. The city uses the results to estimate the habits of all residents. What is the main concern?
choices: Selecting every fifth person automatically makes the sample a census.
Gym visitors may not represent all city residents’ exercise habits.
Exercise habits cannot be measured with a survey.
Every gym visitor exercises exactly the same amount.
explanation: The sampling frame excludes many residents and may overrepresent frequent exercisers. Systematic selection within the gym does not remove this coverage bias.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: Two classes try different review methods. One class is taught by an experienced teacher and the other by a new teacher. Students were not randomly assigned. Which variable is confounded with review method?
choices: The number of review methods, which is two
The fact that the students attend classes
Teacher experience
The use of an examination as an outcome
explanation: Teacher experience varies together with method, so the score difference cannot be cleanly attributed to review method. A confound is an alternative explanatory difference between groups.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: Researchers give one group of plants fertilizer and leave another group untreated. Both groups receive equal light and water. What is the untreated group’s role?
choices: It ensures every plant grows to the same height.
It eliminates the need to measure growth.
It proves fertilizer is harmful before the experiment begins.
It provides a comparison for evaluating the effect of fertilizer.
explanation: A control group provides a baseline against which the treatment outcome can be compared. It does not predetermine the result or replace measurement.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: A company tests a new app using only employees who volunteered. Employees are randomly assigned to new or old versions. Which limitation remains even if the comparison between versions is well controlled?
choices: The volunteers may not represent the app’s wider user population.
Random assignment cannot support any comparison between app versions.
Every employee must use both versions simultaneously.
The two versions must produce identical outcomes.
explanation: Random assignment can strengthen internal causal inference, but volunteer recruitment may limit generalization. Assignment does not repair a nonrepresentative sampling frame.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: A pollster randomly contacts 1,000 residents, but only 150 respond. Which question is most relevant when evaluating possible nonresponse bias?
choices: Did every respondent choose a different answer?
Do respondents differ from nonrespondents in opinions related to the poll’s topic?
Was the original contact list longer than the final sample?
Can the 150 responses be added together?
explanation: Nonresponse bias concerns systematic topic-related differences between those who respond and those who do not. Merely knowing that the sample shrank does not identify the direction or existence of bias.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: An experiment compares two instruction manuals. Participants know which is advertised as the improved manual, and they rate ease of use afterward. Which change would most directly reduce expectation-related bias?
choices: Tell all participants that the new manual must be superior.
Allow only participants who helped write the new manual.
Conceal which manual is the advertised improved version.
Remove every question about ease of use.
explanation: Blinding the advertised status reduces the influence of expectations while preserving the outcome being evaluated. The other choices either increase bias or eliminate the intended assessment.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: A researcher records that towns with more public parks also have higher property prices and concludes that building any park will increase nearby prices. What most directly weakens this causal conclusion?
choices: Public parks can be counted.
Property prices differ from one home to another.
The researcher recorded information from more than one town.
Income or other town characteristics could influence both park availability and property prices.
explanation: A common cause could create the association without parks alone causing the price difference. Basic measurability and ordinary variation do not by themselves explain the causal limitation.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: A factory wants an estimate of the proportion of defective items in today’s full production. Which plan best supports a representative estimate?
choices: Randomly select items throughout today’s entire production run.
Inspect only the first ten items made after maintenance.
Inspect only items a worker thinks look unusual.
Inspect only items that customers have returned.
explanation: Random coverage throughout the target run avoids selecting only special periods or visibly unusual cases. The other plans systematically favor particular items.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: Researchers randomly assign students to one of two practice routines, but many students do not follow their assigned routine. Why does this matter when interpreting the experiment?
choices: Noncompliance proves both routines are identical.
Noncompliance can make the effect of assignment differ from the effect of actually following the routine.
Random assignment means following the routine is irrelevant.
Noncompliance guarantees a representative national sample.
explanation: Randomization defines an assignment comparison. When actual behavior differs from assignment, that comparison does not directly identify the effect of consistently following a routine without additional assumptions.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: A survey asks, “Do you agree that our excellent new library deserves more funding?” What is the main concern about this wording?
choices: It requires respondents to calculate a percentage.
It randomly assigns respondents to funding plans.
It may encourage favorable responses by describing the library positively.
It prevents anyone from expressing an opinion.
explanation: Calling the library excellent introduces a leading evaluation that may affect responses. Neutral wording would better separate respondents’ views from the question’s framing.

skill: Evaluating statistical claims: observational studies and experiments
prompt: An observational study finds a positive association between tutoring hours and test scores. A separate randomized experiment also finds that assigned tutoring raises average scores. Which statement is best supported?
choices: Both studies prove tutoring raises every individual’s score by the same amount.
The observational study is automatically more causal because it observes real behavior.
The experiment proves that prior motivation cannot affect test scores.
The randomized experiment supplies stronger evidence for a causal tutoring effect than the observational association alone.
explanation: Random assignment better separates tutoring from preexisting differences. An average causal effect does not imply identical individual effects or rule out other influences on scores.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
prompt: Data set A is 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. Data set B is 30, 32, 34, 36, 38. How do their standard deviations compare?
choices: They are equal.
B’s standard deviation is 20 greater.
B’s standard deviation is three times A’s.
A’s standard deviation is zero.
explanation: B adds 20 to each value in A. Both the values and the mean shift equally, leaving every deviation from the mean unchanged.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
prompt: Data set B is formed by multiplying every value in data set A by 3. Data set A has standard deviation 4. What is B’s standard deviation?
explanation: Scaling each observation by 3 scales all distances from the mean by 3, so the standard deviation becomes 3×4=12. Variance, rather than standard deviation, scales by 9.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
prompt: Which data set has a standard deviation of zero?
explanation: Standard deviation is zero exactly when every observation equals the mean. Only the all-7 data set has no spread.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
prompt: A data set is 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. A second data set replaces 12 with 120. Which statement is true?
choices: The mean and median both remain unchanged.
The median increases to 11.
The mean decreases because the range increases.
The mean increases, but the median remains 10.
explanation: The ordered middle value is still 10. The sum increases by 108, so the mean increases by 108/5. The extreme replacement changes mean and spread without changing the median.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
prompt: Two five-value data sets both have mean 20. Set A is 18, 19, 20, 21, 22. Set B is 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Which has greater standard deviation?
choices: Set B
Set A
Their standard deviations must be equal because their means are equal.
Both standard deviations are zero.
explanation: Every deviation in B is five times the corresponding deviation in A, so B has five times the standard deviation. Equal centers do not imply equal spread.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
prompt: A data set has minimum 14 and maximum 53. What is its range?
explanation: Range is maximum minus minimum: 53−14=39. It describes the span between the extreme observations.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
prompt: A data set has mean 15. Every value is transformed by the rule y = 2x + 7. Which statement correctly describes the transformed data?
choices: Its mean is 30, and its standard deviation increases by 7.
Its mean is 22, and its standard deviation is unchanged.
Its mean is 37, and its standard deviation is twice the original standard deviation.
Its mean is 37, and its standard deviation increases by 7.
explanation: The mean transforms as 2(15)+7=37. Multiplication by 2 doubles spread; adding 7 shifts all values without changing spread.

skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
prompt: A frequency table gives value 2 with frequency 4, value 5 with frequency 7, and value 9 with frequency 3. What is the mode?
explanation: The mode is the observed value with greatest frequency. Value 5 appears 7 times, more than the other values. Frequency 7 is not itself the modal data value.
